title: Suppression of Non-Hermitian Skin Effect by Pseudomagnetic Field in Honeycomb Lattice
abstract: Magnetic suppression of the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) offers a viable route for its control. While the NHSE has been realized in various classical-wave platforms, only pseudomagnetic fields (PMFs), which preserve time-reversal symmetry, can be engineered in such systems; however, their interplay with the NHSE remains underexplored. Here, we investigate this interplay in a non-Hermitian honeycomb lattice by considering two distinct mechanisms for generating PMFs: monotonically increasing strain and spatially modulated gain and loss. We show that in both scenarios, PMFs can efficiently suppress the NHSE by driving skin modes into the bulk, accompanied by a reduction of the skin topological area and a contraction of the complex-energy spectrum under periodic boundary conditions. This mechanism is insensitive to boundary details and holds for various edge terminations, including zigzag, bearded, armchair, and twig edges. Our results establish PMFs as a versatile and effective means to control the NHSE, and point toward feasible implementations in a broad range of artificial platforms, including photonic and acoustic metamaterials as well as topolectrical circuits.
summary: This paper explores controlling the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect (NHSE) in honeycomb lattices by introducing Pseudomagnetic Fields (PMFs). The authors demonstrate that PMFs, generated via strain or gain/loss modulation, effectively suppress the NHSE by confining bulk states rather than localizing them at boundaries. This establishes PMFs as a powerful and general tool for engineering wave dynamics in artificial metamaterials.
main_problem: The study investigates methods to control the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect (NHSE) using engineered Pseudomagnetic Fields (PMFs). The goal is to show that PMFs provide a robust, symmetry-preserving mechanism for suppressing this localization.
main_result: In both strain-induced and gain/loss-modulated scenarios, PMFs efficiently suppress the NHSE by driving localized skin modes into the bulk spectrum. This control mechanism is shown to be versatile and insensitive to specific boundary terminations.
method: The analysis uses tight-binding models on a honeycomb lattice, analyzing spectral properties (like topological area) under Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC) versus Open Boundary Conditions (OBC). The suppression is diagnosed by observing the contraction of the complex energy spectrum.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a non-Hermitian honeycomb lattice Hamiltonian. PMFs are generated either through monotonically increasing strain or via spatially modulated gain and loss terms, which induce an effective pseudo-gauge field.
key_observables: Suppression of NHSE (skin modes moving into the bulk), reduction of the skin topological area, and contraction of the complex-energy spectrum under PBC.
important_parameters: Strain magnitude ($\alpha$), modulation parameter ($ eta$), lattice hopping amplitudes ($t$, $\delta_x$, $\delta_y$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on treating the system in the long-wavelength limit, allowing for a locally translationally invariant description (momentum space).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate PMF realization via strain and gain/loss; they compare band structures under different conditions; and show spatial wave function intensity profiles demonstrating bulk localization induced by the PMF.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the NHSE problem, details two distinct mechanisms for generating time-reversal symmetric PMFs (strain and gain/loss), analyzes the spectral consequences of these fields on the honeycomb lattice Hamiltonian, and concludes by establishing PMFs as a general control tool for wave localization.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems because it provides concrete theoretical models—using engineered non-Hermiticity (gain/loss) or geometric strain—to actively manipulate topological edge states, which is a key area in modern condensed matter theory and photonics.
